DDT really? I never thought not liking DDT made you racist.

"no one ever got sick from DDT"

I'm going to call bullshit

DDT really?

Yes actually really. Malaria is significantly worse than DDT. Nearly a million people die each year from malaria. It's a very easy thing to die from. DDT isn't good for you... it's a pesticide after all. I don't use hornet spray as a dessert topping. But very few people ever get sick from DDT despite extensive use.

Between 1947 - 1949 we eradicated malaria in the USA using DDT, mortality rates went from 400 cases and 60 deaths per million to essentially zero. In 1949 we declared malaria eradicated but we kept spraying for another couple years to make sure the problem didn't recur and to handle any local outbreaks, the CDC finally stopped it's involvement in DDT spraying in 1952. Today there's almost no cases of malaria outside of people getting sick in other countries.

Once we had eradicated malaria we got a bit hysterical over the largely hypothetical health risks of the pesticide that made it possible. That makes sense, once you've handled a disease that kills thousands you can worry about more subtle risks measured in parts per million. We banned DDT in the states and switched from having the CDC assist other nations use DDT to eradicate malaria to discouraging it's use even in nations that desperately needed it.

When Sri Lanka began using DDT in 1948 they had 2.8 million cases of malaria. By 1963 there were 17 cases of malaria. In 1964 DDT was banned in Sri Lanka. To be fair this was partly the result of complacency thinking they had eradicated the disease. But, it was also the result of the hysteria over it's use. By 1969 they were back up to 2.5million cases of malaria. The Sri Lankan's of course ignored the west's proscriptions on DDT and went back to spraying.

But by then it was too late. Just like stopping anti-biotics mid-course because you're feeling better (and your friend America is telling you to go all organic) a less than lethal treatment creates a resistant strain. The remaining population of mosquitos both still carried the disease, and now were highly resistant to DDT. New, more expensive and less effective pesticides (and still not stuff you'd use for a dessert topping) had to be used. Sri Lanka still has significant issues with malaria though with a lot of work they've made huge progress since the rebound after banning DDT.

I don't think western environmentalists were racists. They were merely parochial: Tightly focussed on the particular problems they cared about and far away from the more severe problems their solutions ended up exacerbating. Still their ignorance and excessive zeal cost hundreds of thousands if not millions of preventable deaths.

This company claims that the reason their cryonic preservation techniques aren't mainstream is because most cryobiologists are unaware of their work. Is it bullshit?

Unfortunately I believe you're presenting a straw man argument.

This quote from the page is the best evidence I found to support your premise:

Most experts in any single field will say that they know of no evidence that cryonics can work. [...] Even though this use of vitrification has been published, it is so uncommon outside of cryonics that only a handful of cryobiologists know it is possible.

However, I think you've misinterpreted this. Let's look at the context!

Myth 4: Experts say cryonics cannot work.

Most experts in any single field will say that they know of no evidence that cryonics can work. That's because cryonics is an interdisciplinary field based on three facts from diverse unrelated sciences. Without all these facts, cryonics seems ridiculous. Unfortunately that makes the number of experts qualified to comment on cryonics very small. For example, very few scientists even know what vitrification is. Fewer still know that vitrification can preserve cell structure of whole organs or whole brains. Even though this use of vitrification has been published, it is so uncommon outside of cryonics that only a handful of cryobiologists know it is possible.

The situation is comparable to the development of space travel before World War II. At that time, "aeronautical experts" were adamant that space travel was impossible. Only Robert Goddard and a few German rocket scientists knew that multi-stage rockets could escape the earth. As is often the case, the experts best qualified to comment on a new field are the experts working in that field. No properly qualified expert has ever said cryonics can't work. The problem is finding experts qualified to comment on cryonics.

From what I understand, they are not claiming that their vitrification technique is not mainstream because most cryobiologists are unaware of it; they are claiming the field of cryonics itself (which is not a 'single field') is not mainstream so experts in other fields are largely uninformed on the subject and thus are unqualified to comment of the viability of what the company is doing.

Also, I believe they are using the terms in quotation marks like "aeronautical experts" and "authorities" ironically. From the page's opening statement:

Unfortunately, much of the news coverage has been based on misconceptions and statements from "authorities" who lack basic information about the field.

I wont go on to deeply examine the claim they are actually making here, but at a preliminary look I don't think it's a flawed argument. I call no bullshit.

Bonus: I spent a lot of time looking into the viability of cryonics before I reassessed the questions premise. I came across an interesting anecdote in a transcript of a 2013 episode of the Skeptics' Guide podcast and they actually speak highly of Alcor, the company in question.

Edit: Actually, on second thought, I retract my hasty 'no bullshit' call on this argument. I won't go as far as calling 'bullshit' on the entire thing (they seem to be citing credible enough journal articles) but just because a field exists and people specialize in it does not lend legitimacy to the practice. For example, just because there are chiropractors who truly believe in and promote chiropractobunk, doesn't mean it works.

Before you call them, connect to your cable modem or mode & router combo with an ethernet cable. A cable directly between the PC you'll be using to troubleshoot and the modem or modem and router combo. TWC support will likely ask you to do this during the call anyway. The rule of discussing connection issues with ISP support: it's always your fault in some way, whether a program you're running or a setting you have enabled, it's always fine on their end and there must be fault with your setup.
